A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Triple-BERT study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices A-F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original ride-dispatch simulation results using Manhattan trip data, including baseline comparisons, ablations, generalization tests and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds reported evaluations using Manhattan and Queens high-volume for-hire vehicle trip data.

M1.justification: The BERT architecture, normalized QK-attention, IDDQN pretraining, centralized TD3 training, action matching and optimization updates are retained. Revised policy explanations and Table 1 descriptions do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Section 4 adds Manhattan high-volume for-hire vehicle data, and Appendix E.5 adds Queens trips. These substantially extend the retained Manhattan yellow-taxi coverage to another service population and a geographically larger, more dispersed demand environment.

E2.justification: The nearest-worker Greedy baseline disappears from Figure 3 and its accompanying description. DeepPool, BMG-Q, HIVES, Enders et al. and CEVD remain evaluated, including in the new FHV comparisons; newly discussed related methods are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: New evaluation settings include 48 half-hour episodes covering July 18, 2024, for Manhattan FHV data, and a Queens scenario with 500 drivers and 2,024 orders. Existing training settings, evaluation metrics and original experimental splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The added FHV and Queens experiments explicitly investigate generalization under changed demand distributions and geographic dispersion. This substantially broadens the existing analyses across dates, fleet sizes and noise types. The positional-embedding and encoder ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 3 changes its reported training count from three to five runs and its shading from fluctuation ranges to standard deviations. Figure 4 newly documents three runs and its averaging, smoothing and shading conventions, without establishing additional runs. Figure 6 retains three-repeat standard-deviation reporting.

E6.justification: New Tables 2 and 8 report six-method, six-metric results: Triple-BERT achieves reward 14,329.74 versus CEVD's 12,556.74 on Manhattan FHV, and 5,577.83 versus BMG-Q's 5,362.00 in Queens. These are new-setting results. Existing tables retain their numerical values, while Figure 3 updates curves and removes Greedy results.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.2 withdraws the claim that normalization guarantees a unique solution. Appendix C recasts the existing power-law mapping as an explicit definition rather than an approximate elasticity assumption. It also introduces elasticity ab for z(x)=ax^b, although its Equation 15 yields b. The principal equations and derivations otherwise remain.

C1.justification: The central claims about centralized SARL, action decomposition, BERT and two-stage training remain. The abstract and introduction retain the headline 11.95% reward improvement, 4.26% increase in served orders and 22.25% pickup-time reduction. New experiments support these contributions without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: The conclusion newly acknowledges vulnerability to centralized single points of failure and discusses importance sampling and offline pretraining as future directions. Added interpretations explain FHV reward variability, Queens pickup penalties and service-rate versus travel-time tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Table 1 newly specifies local versus global reward use for the evaluated methods, adding explicit technical documentation without establishing changed training objectives. Hardware, model hyperparameters, optimization schedules, software and code/data access statements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix F expands from a brief dispatch review into separate ride-sharing and cooperative-MARL discussions. It adds substantial positioning against mean-field, counterfactual, value-decomposition, consensus and communication approaches, alongside pricing, repositioning and fairness research, and explains their alleged limitations at large agent counts.

P1.justification: Appendix F is extensively rewritten and reorganized into two subsections. The actor-policy explanation and Appendix C are also rewritten, figure explanations are expanded, and terminology is corrected, including the abstract's erroneous MARL abbreviation for single-agent RL. The overall main-section sequence remains.

P2.justification: v2 adds two result tables, expands Table 1 with reward-type and training-stage information, and redraws Figure 3 with revised axes, legend and uncertainty display. Figures 1, 2 and 4 gain explanatory captions. Other figure artwork and existing table structures are largely retained.

improvement.justification: The FHV and Queens evaluations broaden empirical support beyond Manhattan yellow taxis, while clearer uncertainty reporting, expanded research context and withdrawal of the uniqueness guarantee improve transparency. These provide a net quality gain, moderated by the new ab-versus-b elasticity error in Appendix C and the otherwise retained policy-gradient derivation.
